title: Accuracy
text:
Float functions give results within 4 units in the last place (ulps) of the correctly rounded result, apart from the exceptions below. Where rustymath gives up a few ulps for real speed or a simpler implementation, the loss is listed below. An exactly representable result need not be returned exactly.



Near its zeros at 1 and 2, lgamma has an absolute error of up to 4 ulps of 2, not 4 ulps of the result. Near its zeros, digamma has an absolute error of up to 4 ulps of 1, and below -20 up to 4 ulps of ln(1 - x).
For a non-whole n and a whole k up to 64, binom and binom_dn are within 2k ulps.
binom_dk has no relative bound near n = 2k, where its two ψ terms cancel.
beta is within 6 ulps at f64. It adds three ln Γ terms. Where two of them have arguments of 10 or more, it computes those two as one difference. For each other term, beta rounds the logarithm of its Lanczos sum to a single f64. That rounding causes the extra error.
A positive whole power from 1 to 8 is computed by squaring and multiplying, without compensation, in the scalar form, and in the slice form when one exponent applies to every item. The rounding error of the step that gives x^k is multiplied by about m/k in x^m. The worst errors measured over every f32 significand and a million random f64 inputs are 4.4 ulps for x^7 and 5.2 for x^8.
Normal and log-normal evaluation of f32 inputs uses f32 arithmetic, with parameters and precomputed coefficients rounded to f32. Here z is the standard score: of x for the normal distribution, and of ln x for the log-normal. Where |z| < 3, their densities are within 12 ulps and their cdfs within 14. As z² grows, the errors grow, to about 80 ulps for densities and 170 for cdfs at |z| = 12. Their quantiles are within 13 ulps, except where the normal quantile, mean + sd·z, is near 0. There cancellation leaves an absolute error of up to 8 ulps of the standard deviation. The log-normal quantile is the exponential of a normal quantile, so this cancellation affects it near a quantile of 1. These figures exclude additional error from parameter rounding and ill-conditioned location/scale transformations.
Uniform, exponential, Cauchy, Laplace, logistic and Weibull evaluation of f32 inputs uses f32 arithmetic too, with parameters and precomputed coefficients rounded to f32. For both f32 and f64, their densities and cdfs are within 4 ulps, with two exceptions. The logistic density at f64 is within 4.4 ulps because of rounding in its exponential, square and quotient. For the Weibull density, z is x/scale. The density is within 4 ulps up to z^shape = 4. Above that, its error grows to about z^shape ulps, such as 15, 50 and 240 ulps at z^shape = 16, 64 and 256. Rounding z^shape before computing e(-zshape) causes that much error, however z^shape is computed. Their quantiles are within 4 ulps, except for the Cauchy, Laplace and logistic laws near a quantile of 0. There the quantile is location + scale·q, where q is the standard law’s quantile. Cancellation in that sum leaves an absolute error of up to 4 ulps of the scale. These figures exclude additional error from parameter rounding, ill-conditioned location/scale transformations, and arguments whose standardized value is subnormal.
The error of a complex function is measured in ulps of the result’s magnitude: |f(z) - exact| is within 4 ulps of |exact|. When one part of the result is much smaller than the other, that part can therefore have a large relative error. Complex ln Γ is measured in ulps of the larger of its magnitude and 2. Rustymath computes complex powers, Γ and binomial coefficients as the exponential of an exponent e, which is w ln z for z^w and ln Γ for Γ and binomial coefficients. Their error is measured in ulps of their magnitude times 1 + max(|e|, 2).





Reproducibility. Floating-point last bits and seeded random draws can differ with batching, fusion, JIT, thread counts, array sizes, execution routes, platforms, builds and runs. A fold such as a sum can combine its items in any order.
Infinities and NaNs. Results involving infinities or NaNs can differ by function, code path and platform. FMA and reassociation can overflow differently near the range limits. Given a NaN argument, a function can return NaN or another argument. The maximum or minimum of several values, whether two arguments or an array’s items, is NaN or the extreme of the values that aren’t NaN: the maximum of 5, NaN and 3 can be 5 or NaN, never 3. Which NaN is returned, and its sign and payload, aren’t promised. Finite accuracy bounds still apply to subnormal results.
The sign of zero. The sign of a zero result can differ by function, code path and platform.

title: rustymath
text:
Rustymath provides fast elementary and special functions, statistics, searching and sorting, random sampling, linear algebra, optimization, polynomials and exact arithmetic in Rust and Python. It is the numerical core of BasedPL.
The Python package needs no NumPy. Its eager operations use the same broadcasting, selection and tolerant-comparison rules as the shared Rust core. For richer array notation, operators and fusion, use BasedPL.
Float functions give results within four units in the last place (ulps) of the correctly rounded result, apart from documented exceptions. Rustymath prioritizes speed over last-bit agreement and reproducibility.

title: rustymath
text:
Install
pip install rustymath
Rust users can add the crate to Cargo.toml. See Using rustymath from Rust for function objects and native bulk routines, build settings, accuracy and speed.

import rustymath as rm

title: rustymath
text:
Arrays and indexing
Functions take Python numbers, nested lists, rustymath arrays or buffer exporters such as NumPy arrays. Broadcasting aligns leading axes. Here rm.add adds the vector’s first item to the matrix’s first row and its second item to the second row:

rm.add([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]], [10, 20])

Array([[11, 12, 13], [24, 25, 26]], dtype=int64)


Arrays and indexing covers construction, dtypes, selection, reshaping, axis names, keys and interoperability.

title: rustymath
text:
Maths and statistics
Real and complex functions operate on whole arrays. The rustymath.mathish namespace provides J-inspired Mathish conventions. Ordinary comparisons are exact:

rm.exp([0., 1, 2]), rm.equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)

(Array([1.0, 2.7182818, 7.3890561], dtype=float64), False)


Maths and statistics covers elementary and special functions, reductions, scans, statistics and tolerant comparison.

title: rustymath
text:
Searching, sorting and selection
unique keeps the order in which values first occur. It also gives each value’s first position (firsts) and count (counts), and for each item the position of its value in values (numbers):

rm.unique([3, 1, 3, 2])

Unique(values=Array([3, 1, 2], dtype=int64), firsts=Array([0, 1, 3], dtype=int64), numbers=Array([0, 1, 0, 2], dtype=int64), counts=Array([2, 1, 1], dtype=int64))


Searching, sorting and selection distinguishes tolerant matching from exact ordering.

title: rustymath
text:
Random numbers and distributions
Distributions provide density, cumulative probability, quantiles and seeded sampling:

normal = rm.distribution.normal()
normal.cdf([-1.96, 0, 1.96]), normal.sample(3, seed=0)

(Array([0.024997895, 0.5, 0.9750021], dtype=float64),
 Array([0.11623959, -0.78285485, -2.3346353], dtype=float64))


Random numbers and distributions covers sampling and probability functions.

title: rustymath
text:
Linear algebra
Solve real or complex systems, including least-norm solutions for singular or non-square matrices:

rm.linalg.solve([[4., 1], [1, 3]], [1., 2])

Array([0.090909091, 0.63636364], dtype=float64)


Linear algebra covers matrix products, reusable factorizations, decompositions and least squares.

title: rustymath
text:
Optimization and iterative solves
Minimize functions, fit parameters by least squares or find roots. Here Brent’s method finds where cos x = x:

rm.optimize.root_scalar(lambda x: rm.cos(x) - x, [0, 1]).root

0.7390851350713886


Optimization and iterative solves also covers matrix-free linear systems.

title: Polynomials, exact arithmetic and number theory
text:
Polynomials
rm.polynomial evaluates polynomials, finds roots, constructs coefficients from roots, differentiates and fits data, under the names of numpy.polynomial.polynomial. Coefficients start from the constant term. Evaluation, construction and derivatives take real or complex arrays. polyvalfromroots(x, roots, m=1) evaluates m(x - r₁)(x - r₂)… directly from the roots, without forming coefficients. The roots of x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 are 1, 2 and 3:

p = rm.polynomial
roots = rm.array([1., 2, 3])
c = p.polyfromroots(roots)
c, p.polyroots(c), p.polyval([0, 4], c), p.polyder(c), p.polyvalfromroots([0, 4], roots)

(Array([-6.0, 11.0, -6.0, 1.0], dtype=float64),
 Array([(1+0j), (2-0j), (3+0j)], dtype=complex128),
 Array([-6.0, 6.0], dtype=float64),
 Array([11.0, -12.0, 3.0], dtype=float64),
 Array([-6.0, 6.0], dtype=float64))


polyfit(x, y, degree) fits coefficients by least squares. Evaluate the fitted line at new points with polyval:

fit = p.polyfit([0., 1, 2, 3], [1.1, 2.9, 5.2, 6.8], 1)
fit, p.polyval([4., 5], fit)

(Array([1.09, 1.94], dtype=float64), Array([8.85, 10.79], dtype=float64))

title: Polynomials, exact arithmetic and number theory
text:
Exact arithmetic
rm.exact computes with integers and fractions.Fraction. It provides rational gcd, lcm, remainder and binomial coefficients, matrix solves, pseudoinverses, determinants, permanents and row reduction, and polynomial construction, evaluation and derivatives. Arguments can be integers, Fractions, nested lists of them, or integer arrays. A result is a Fraction, or nested lists of Fractions for an array. Matrix functions take one matrix, not a stack of matrices.

from fractions import Fraction


rm.exact.solve([[2, 1], [1, 2]], [Fraction(1, 2), 0]), rm.exact.binom(Fraction(3, 2), 2)

([Fraction(1, 3), Fraction(-1, 6)], Fraction(3, 8))


An underdetermined system has many solutions. exact.solve chooses the one with least Euclidean norm. pinv gives a matrix that you can reuse for the same least-norm solve:

a = [[1, 1]]
rm.exact.solve(a, [1]), rm.exact.pinv(a)

([Fraction(1, 2), Fraction(1, 2)], [[Fraction(1, 2)], [Fraction(1, 2)]])


To reduce an augmented system, call rm.exact.echelon with columns set to the number of unknowns. The result’s .rows contains the nonzero reduced rows, and its .pivots contains their pivot columns. .determinant is the signed product of the unscaled pivots. It equals the determinant of the coefficient matrix when that matrix is square and full-rank:

e = rm.exact.echelon([[2, 1, 1], [1, 2, 0]], columns=2)
e.rows, e.pivots, e.determinant

([[Fraction(1, 1), Fraction(0, 1), Fraction(2, 3)],
  [Fraction(0, 1), Fraction(1, 1), Fraction(-1, 3)]],
 [0, 1],
 Fraction(3, 1))


The permanent sums the same products as the determinant without permutation signs. rm.linalg.permanent computes it in floating point:

square = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
rm.exact.det(square), rm.exact.permanent(square)

(Fraction(-2, 1), Fraction(10, 1))


Rational gcd and remainder compute without rounding. Exact polynomial operations use the same constant-first coefficients:

r = [Fraction(1, 2), Fraction(3, 4)]
rm.exact.gcd(r, Fraction(1, 3)), rm.exact.remainder(r, Fraction(1, 3)), rm.exact.polyval(r, [1, 0, Fraction(1, 2)])

([Fraction(1, 6), Fraction(1, 12)],
 [Fraction(1, 6), Fraction(1, 12)],
 [Fraction(9, 8), Fraction(41, 32)])

title: Polynomials, exact arithmetic and number theory
text:
Number theory
rm.number_theory tests primality, factorises, finds neighbouring primes and gives Euler’s totient for arbitrary-size nonnegative Python integers. Primality testing uses Baillie–PSW. No composite below 2^64 passes it. A larger number that passes is a probable prime, and no composite is known to pass. Long calls stop on Ctrl-C:

nt = rm.number_theory
nt.factor(2**64 + 1), nt.prime_count(10**8), nt.next_prime(10**20)

([(274177, 1), (67280421310721, 1)], 5761455, 100000000000000000039)


primes(start, stop) lists the primes in the half-open interval [start, stop), and primes(stop) starts from zero. primes, prime_count and factorial take unsigned 64-bit arguments. The primes returned by primes must fit in int64. number_theory.factorial returns an exact Python integer, whereas rm.factorial returns a floating-point number:

nt.primes(100, 120), nt.is_prime(101), nt.totient(36), nt.factorial(30)

(Array([101, 103, 107, 109, 113], dtype=int64),
 True,
 12,
 265252859812191058636308480000000)

title: Polynomials, exact arithmetic and number theory
text:
Mixed radix
rm.encode and rm.decode are aliases for rm.integer.encode and rm.integer.decode. Digits occupy the last axis, most significant first. Bases [0, 60, 60] split seconds into hours, minutes and seconds. A leading zero in the radix leaves the hours unbounded:

seconds = rm.array([3661, 86399])
hms = rm.encode([0, 60, 60], seconds)
hms, rm.decode([0, 60, 60], hms)

(Array([[1, 1, 1], [23, 59, 59]], dtype=int64),
 Array([3661, 86399], dtype=int64))


Integer decoding wraps at int64’s range, as BasedPL’s ⊥ does, and integer encoding raises OverflowError when a quotient doesn’t fit int64. polynomial.decode and exact.decode accept bases and digits of any type with the field operations, such as Fraction. Fractional seconds stay exact:

rm.exact.decode([0, 60, 60], [1, 1, Fraction(3, 2)])

Fraction(7323, 2)

from types import SimpleNamespace

title: Optimization and iterative solves
text:
Minimization and scalar roots
rm.optimize uses SciPy’s function names. minimize runs Brent’s method, Nelder–Mead, Powell’s method, L-BFGS or differential evolution. If method is omitted, minimize chooses a method based on the number of variables, whether jac supplies a gradient and whether bounds are given. root_scalar finds a zero of a function of one variable by Brent’s method, within a bracket or by stepping outward from a start. Here Nelder–Mead finds the minimum of Rosenbrock’s function, at (1, 1), and Brent’s method finds where cos x = x:

rosen = lambda x: (1-x[0])**2 + 100*(x[1]-x[0]**2)**2
rm.optimize.minimize(rosen, [-1.2, 1]).x, rm.optimize.root_scalar(lambda x: rm.cos(x) - x, [0, 1]).root

(Array([1.0, 1.0], dtype=float64), 0.7390851350713886)


jac supplies the gradient. Here, supplying it selects L-BFGS. Results report the best point, its objective value, the number of evaluations and whether the stopping test passed:

rosen_grad = lambda x: [-2*(1-x[0]) - 400*x[0]*(x[1]-x[0]**2), 200*(x[1]-x[0]**2)]
minimum = rm.optimize.minimize(rosen, [-1.2, 1], jac=rosen_grad)
minimum.x, minimum.fun, minimum.nfev, minimum.success

(Array([1.0, 1.0], dtype=float64), 2.6802658590531843e-27, 53, True)


Differential evolution searches within finite bounds. popsize sets the number of population members per variable; maxfev caps objective evaluations, including those of the final local refinement, called polishing. With vectorized=True, the objective receives an array of shape (variables, candidates) and returns one value per column. Rosenbrock’s expression works unchanged on both single points and columns. seed selects the random sequence:

bounded = rm.optimize.minimize(rosen, [-1.2, 1], method='differential-evolution',
    bounds=[(-2, 2), (-1, 3)], vectorized=True, options={'seed': 7, 'popsize': 8, 'maxfev': 2000})
bounded.x, bounded.fun, bounded.nfev, bounded.success

(Array([1.0, 1.0], dtype=float64), 3.404388655577681e-16, 1465, True)

title: Optimization and iterative solves
text:
Fitting residuals
least_squares minimizes a sum of squared residuals using Levenberg–Marquardt. jac returns a Jacobian with one row per residual and one column per parameter. least_squares uses forward differences when jac is omitted. Here the fit recovers a = 2 and b = 0.3 from five points on y = a e^(bx):

t = rm.array([0., 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2])
residuals = lambda p: p[0]*rm.exp(p[1]*t) - 2*rm.exp(0.3*t)
jacobian = lambda p: rm.stack([rm.exp(p[1]*t), p[0]*t*rm.exp(p[1]*t)], axis=1)
fit = rm.optimize.least_squares(residuals, [1, 1], jac=jacobian)
fit.x, fit.cost, fit.success

(Array([2.0, 0.3], dtype=float64), 3.468843267386382e-27, True)

title: Optimization and iterative solves
text:
Matrix-free linear systems
The linear solvers take an array or an operator with shape and matvec, such as a SciPy LinearOperator. For array inputs, the linear solvers compute matrix-vector products in Rust. Operators compute matrix-vector products without storing the matrix.







Solver
Matrix requirement




cg
Symmetric positive definite


minres
Symmetric


gmres
General square


cgls, lsmr
Rectangular or square; operators also supply rmatvec for transpose products



cgls applies CG to the normal equations without forming A.T @ A. lsmr uses MINRES on the normal equations. cgls is not a Golub–Kahan LSQR implementation.
M is a preconditioner that approximates the inverse matrix, or the inverse of A.T @ A for least squares. M must be symmetric positive definite unless the solver is gmres. GMRES applies M on the right, solving A M y = b and returning x = M y. SciPy’s GMRES uses left preconditioning.
This example fits a line using an operator instead of constructing its five-by-two design matrix. The preconditioner M is the inverse of A.T @ A’s diagonal. normr is the norm of the residual b - A x, which isn’t zero when no line fits the points exactly:

positions = rm.arange(5, dtype='float64')
operator = SimpleNamespace(shape=(5, 2), matvec=lambda v: v[0] + v[1]*positions,
    rmatvec=lambda u: [rm.sum(u), rm.sum(positions*u)])
preconditioner = rm.diag([1/len(positions), 1/rm.sum(positions**2)])
line = rm.optimize.cgls(operator, [1., 2.9, 5.2, 6.8, 9.1], M=preconditioner)
line.x, line.normr, line.nmatvec, line.success

(Array([0.98, 2.01], dtype=float64), 0.31464265445104594, 8, True)

title: Random numbers and distributions
text:
A persistent generator
default_rng(seed) creates one generator whose state advances across calls. A size tuple gives the output shape. Reuse the generator for different distributions:

rng = rm.default_rng(42)
draws = rng.normal(size=(3, 2))
draws, draws.mean(axis=0), rng.sample(rm.distribution.beta(2, 3), 5)

(Array([[-1.0920367, -0.30040901], [-0.78924237, 0.52985647], [-2.2347094, 1.3224215]], dtype=float64),
 Array([-1.3719962, 0.51728964], dtype=float64),
 Array([0.16794595, 0.31556707, 0.25183041, 0.32702751, 0.60316242], dtype=float64))


integers draws from the half-open interval [low, high). choice and permutation sample or permute along the first axis, or over range(n) when passed an integer n. Here the two selected items are whole rows:

rng.integers(0, 10, size=4), rng.choice(draws, size=2, replace=False)

(Array([5, 3, 0, 4], dtype=int64),
 Array([[-1.0920367, -0.30040901], [-2.2347094, 1.3224215]], dtype=float64))


The seed initializes the generator’s state. It uses rustymath’s random number generation, shared with its Rust core, and does not reproduce NumPy’s random sequences. Draws can differ with thread count or scheduling, execution route, platform or build.
multivariate_normal(mean, cov, size) draws from a multivariate normal distribution by multiplying standard normal draws by the Cholesky factor of cov. It takes a real mean vector and a real positive-definite covariance matrix. Neither may have axis keys or names. It returns float64 samples whose final axis holds the components. If cov isn’t positive definite, its Cholesky factor is NaN, and so are the samples.

rng.multivariate_normal([1., 2.], [[4., 1.], [1., 3.]], size=3)

Array([[-0.90930908, 2.008366], [4.0249491, 6.4071364], [-1.7609395, 1.433404]], dtype=float64)

title: Random numbers and distributions
text:
Probability functions
rm.distribution constructors return objects with pdf, cdf, quantile and sample. cdf(x) is the probability of a value at most x. Subtract cdf(x) from one to get the probability of a value greater than x. Supply seed to start the sample from a chosen generator state:

n = rm.distribution.normal()
n.cdf([-1.96, 0, 1.96]), 1 - n.cdf(1.96), n.quantile(0.975), n.sample(3, seed=0)

(Array([0.024997895, 0.5, 0.9750021], dtype=float64),
 0.024997895148220484,
 1.9599639845400538,
 Array([0.11623959, -0.78285485, -2.3346353], dtype=float64))


For a discrete distribution, pdf(k) gives the probability mass at k. With an expected rate of 2 arrivals per interval, poisson(2) gives the probabilities of 0 to 3 arrivals, the probability of at least 4, and the 95th-percentile count:

arrivals = rm.distribution.poisson(2)
arrivals.pdf([0, 1, 2, 3]), 1 - arrivals.cdf(3), arrivals.quantile(0.95)

(Array([0.13533528, 0.27067057, 0.27067057, 0.18044704], dtype=float64),
 0.14287653950145296,
 5.0)

title: Using rustymath from Rust
text:
Add rustymath to your Cargo.toml:
[dependencies]
rustymath = "0.1"
On x86-64, build for a recent CPU, with -C target-cpu=x86-64-v3 or -C target-cpu=native. You can set it once in .cargo/config.toml:
[target.'cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")']
rustflags = ["-C", "target-cpu=x86-64-v3"]
Rust’s default x86-64 target has no fused multiply-add and no vector instruction for floor or trunc. Without the setting, rustymath multiplies and adds separately. Some of its loops also run one item at a time.
Free functions such as exp are generic over f32, f64 and half::f16. The compiler inlines such a function into the loop that calls it, and vectorizes that loop:
use half::f16;
use rustymath::exp;

let e64 = exp(1.0f64); // 2.718281828459045
let e32 = exp(1.0f32); // 2.718282
let e16 = exp(f16::from_f32(1.0)); // 2.719
For whole arrays, resolve a formula object such as Pow to an operation::Kernel. Kernel::map reads each argument through a ReadPlan and replaces the contents of an output Buffer. Here map reads x in order through ReadPlan::input, and repeats the exponent’s one item through ReadPlan::copy:
use rustymath::{
    Pow, agreement::{Binding, Mapping, Missing, Read, ReadPlan}, buffer::{Buffer, Element},
    domain::Variant, operation::{Kernel, Settings}, tolerant::Tolerance,
};

let x = [1.5, 2.0, 3.0];
let exponent = [2.0];
let sources = [Binding::full(f64::view(&x)), Binding::full(f64::view(&exponent))];
let plans = [ReadPlan::input(0, 3), ReadPlan::copy(1, 1, Mapping::Single, 3, Missing::Default)];
let reads = plans.each_ref().map(|plan| Read { sources: &sources, plan });
let pow = Kernel::resolve(Pow, Variant::checked(f64::DTYPE), [f64::DTYPE; 2]).unwrap();
let settings = Settings { tolerance: Tolerance::EXACT };
let mut squares = Buffer::with_capacity(pow.result_dtype(), 3);
pow.map(&reads, 0..3, settings, &mut squares).unwrap();
assert_eq!(f64::vec(squares).unwrap(), [2.25, 4.0, 9.0]);
facts::Formula defines each formula object’s numerical rules, supported kinds, validity, ranges and derivatives. Kernel::resolve selects the kernel’s computing and result dtypes. Kernel::of selects a formula from a runtime facts::Op. Kernels use native bulk routines where a formula supplies them, and otherwise run its item formula. Their map, fold_read, fold_pieces and scan methods take shared agreement::Read plans. The kernel methods real, integers, complex and exact evaluate scalar arguments with the kernel’s numerical policy and return a Result.
use rustymath::{Exp, domain::Variant, operation::Kernel, buffer::{DType, FloatWidth, Width}};

let double = DType::Float(FloatWidth::F64);
let exp = Kernel::resolve(Exp, Variant::checked(double), [DType::Integer(Width::I32)]).unwrap();
assert_eq!(exp.variant().dtype, double);
Sin, Cos and Tan use a short argument reduction and polynomials for arguments up to 2^23 at f64, or 2^20 at f32. An object’s repair predicate marks arguments of larger magnitude. Its native slice driver applies the object’s scalar repair routine to those items before returning the results. Kernel::ranged omits repair when the same predicate is proved false over the supplied ranges.
atan2(y, x) and a kernel of Atan2 give the angle of the point (x, y), from -π to π. y comes first, as in f64::atan2.
divide(x, y) divides complex numbers and is inlined into the caller’s loop, like the other free functions. When both arguments are real, divide divides them as reals: a real zero divisor gives ±∞ or NaN, with an imaginary part of 0. The |y|² in its formula overflows when |y| is beyond about 1e154 at f64 and 1e19 at f32.


The tolerant module has APL’s tolerant comparison: x equals y when |x - y| is less than the tolerance times the larger of |x| and |y|. Its formula objects, such as Equal, Less, Floor, Residue and Gcd, hold a Tolerance. operation::Settings supplies the tolerance for a kernel execution. With Tolerance::EXACT, a kernel chooses ordinary comparison once for the whole call. A comparison kernel produces Boolean array results; its scalar real method represents true and false as 1 and 0:
use rustymath::{
    buffer::Element, domain::Variant, operation::{Kernel, Settings}, tolerant::{Equal, Tolerance},
};

let equal = Kernel::resolve(Equal(Tolerance::DEFAULT), Variant::checked(f64::DTYPE), [f64::DTYPE; 2]).unwrap();
let settings = Settings { tolerance: Tolerance::DEFAULT };
let same = [0.3, 0.1 + 0.2, 0.31].map(|x| equal.real(&[x, 0.3], settings).unwrap());
assert_eq!(same, [1.0, 1.0, 0.0]);

create: filled arrays and integer or floating ranges, evenly spaced values and logarithmically spaced values.
stats: means, two-pass variance and standard deviation, weighted averages, elementwise p-norms, covariance, correlation and histograms. Axes prepares reductions over selected axes. Complex variance and norms return real values.

Its functions that take a View support the same dtypes as BasedPL and the Python package. Ordering compares floats exactly, treats signed zeros as equal and puts NaNs last in ascending order.

DType names the type: Booleans, integers of four widths (Width), floats of three (FloatWidth), complex numbers of two (ComplexWidth), or characters. interrupt: the process’s interrupt check. A frontend installs one with install. Long computations call check between steps, about every BETWEEN_CHECKS items, and stop if it returns an Interrupt or Timeout error. Until a frontend installs a check, check always succeeds.

When a binary registers Guard as its global allocator, Rust aborts the process if an allocation would take the total size of its large allocations past the process’s limit. An axis of length 1 repeats along its partner. If both layouts have keys for an axis, the result uses the union of those keys. Agreement is generic over its layout type, so callers can use map_layout to carry their own data on layouts. Frames pairs the frames of any number of arguments to a function that operates on their trailing axes, such as matrices in a stack. For each result cell, it gives the corresponding cell of each argument.

gather: copying a slice’s items into a buffer by position. For a convolution, the kernel is reversed. correlate runs these plans through an Inner pair’s inner_mapped. Float and complex PlusTimes read the windows a block at a time. overlap_add adds each frame back where its window was read. This is the transpose of taking windows.

Loops that call either vectorize on every target. AVX2 and wasm lack a vector instruction for conversion between f64 and 64-bit integers. Like elementary functions, the special functions have free functions and objects at the crate root. These include gamma, lgamma, digamma, erf, erfc, their inverses, binom with its slopes binom_dn and binom_dk, the incomplete gamma and beta functions and Lambert W.
Add, Subtract, Multiply and the other arithmetic objects at the crate root implement Formula. Kernel runs these arithmetic objects at every float, complex and integer type, using the checking and wrapping policy specified by its Variant. For unbounded rationals, call Kernel::exact, which delegates to Formula::exact.

Functions on f16 compute in f32 and round once. IEEE 754 conformance for infinities, NaNs and signed zeros is not promised. The tests compare finite results with references at every f16 input, at samples of f32 and f64 inputs, and at published hard cases.
Where the target has a fused multiply-add instruction, as on AArch64 and on x86-64 with FMA, the functions use it. Elsewhere, as in wasm, they multiply and add separately, because calling a software fma would prevent the compiler from vectorizing the loop. The constant FUSED is true where the target uses fused multiply-add. The modules fused and unfused contain every function again, with fused multiply-add always on or always off. In a loop compiled with FMA for itself, such as an AVX2 version that your program chooses at run time, call fused. Either way, results stay within 4 ulps of the correctly rounded result, apart from the documented exceptions.
General powers and roots use compensated native block algorithms. At f64, logarithms and exponentials use tables. Exceptional inputs take the scalar repair path. Cheap constant powers, square roots and cube roots use specialized formulas.

When a binary registers Guard as its global allocator, Rust aborts the process if an allocation would take the total size of its large allocations past the process’s limit. The limit defaults to half of physical memory and can be changed with set_limit. Before an allocation, layout::generated_len calls admit, which returns a Limit error if the array would pass the limit.
layout: array shapes, axis keys and names, and their limits. Shape holds an array’s axis lengths. Keys names the positions on one axis. Layout pairs a shape with keys and a name for each axis. Layout::axis_named finds an axis by its name. position converts an index to a position within an axis of a given length, counting from the end when the index is negative. Lanes describes an array’s items as lanes along one axis. It provides each item’s offset and the dims that rustymath’s axis functions take. element_count and generated_len count an array’s items and enforce the limits of MAX_RANK axes and MAX_GENERATED_ELEMENTS items. generated_len also enforces the memory guard’s limit. strides gives the distance between neighbouring items along each axis.
agreement: broadcasting by BasedPL’s rule. Agreement::new pairs the axes of two layouts: axes with the same name first, then the rest from the front. If every axis of the left layout pairs and the right layout has more axes, the result uses the right layout’s axis order. Otherwise, the left layout’s axes come first. An axis of length 1 repeats along its partner. If both layouts have keys for an axis, the result uses the union of those keys. The result is the paired layout and a Mapping for each argument, which gives the argument’s offset for each result position. blocks runs a kernel over two slices using an agreement, passing contiguous runs whole. expanded reads one argument’s items for a range of result positions. Agreement is generic over its layout type, so callers can use map_layout to carry their own data on layouts. Frames pairs the frames of any number of arguments to a function that operates on their trailing axes, such as matrices in a stack. For each result cell, it gives the corresponding cell of each argument.
random: uniform floats, bounded integers and sampling without replacement. roll, units, below and deal draw through a caller’s mutable rand::Rng.
gather: copying a slice’s items into a buffer by position. It provides cycle, repeat, positions set in a mask, take at indices, windows, walk along a pattern of Steps with fills, and scatter at offsets. Each applies the caller’s conversion to each item. walk also takes Same, which copies whole slices of one type. Steps::reach gives the source offset of one item of a walk. Steps::run gives the source offset of a run of items that lie in order in the source. Steps::through composes two walks into one. Steps::per_axis gives a walk one entry for each axis of its result. Steps::spreads tells whether an entry repeats an offset or gives a fill, and Steps::rereads whether two entries walk one source axis, as overlapping windows do.
structure: plans for structural operations. A Plan holds the result’s Layout and the Steps that walk follows to copy the result’s items from the source. select applies independent axis selectors for positions, ranges, index arrays and inserted axes. Index arrays are paired in one of two ways: all of them by broadcasting, as BasedPL’s .[] reads them, or only those that share an axis name, as BasedPL’s ⌷ reads them. addressed gives the axis that each selector selects along. take takes or drops items. rotate rotates or reverses an axis, using one count or one count for each lane. transpose sends axes to new positions. catenate gives the layout of two arrays joined along an axis. Windows plans windows over leading axes, centred on each position of a padded axis. An Edge mode sets how the plan reads past the axis’s ends. Walk describes how a copy walks its source, giving the source axis that each entry walks. For the entries along one source axis, read and range give what they read as windows: where the windows start, and each entry’s length and move. Walk::windows recognises a copy of windows laid out by Windows::plan without padding. It gives each axis’s frames, window size and move. Transpose gives the kernel that adds a copy’s cotangent back to its source: a sum along its spread axes, then reads that send each item back, overlap-add for windows that move by more than 1, or a scatter-add. Each plan checks its arguments. In each plan’s result, axis keys and names stay with their positions.
signal: correlations and convolutions, which slide a kernel along an array’s leading axes, and overlap-add. correlation gives the plans used to read a correlation: the array with the fills added by its Mode, the array’s windows, and the kernel. For a convolution, the kernel is reversed. correlate runs these plans through an Inner pair’s inner_mapped. Float and complex PlusTimes read the windows a block at a time. overlap_add adds each frame back where its window was read. This is the transpose of taking windows.
convert: int converts a whole float to an integer type. It gives None outside the type’s range, and for i64 beyond a magnitude of 2^51 - 1. float converts an integer to the nearest float. Loops that call either vectorize on every target. AVX2 and wasm lack a vector instruction for conversion between f64 and 64-bit integers. On those targets a loop that converts with as runs one item at a time.

Like elementary functions, the special functions have free functions and objects at the crate root. These include gamma, lgamma, digamma, erf, erfc, their inverses, binom with its slopes binom_dn and binom_dk, the incomplete gamma and beta functions and Lambert W.
Add, Subtract, Multiply and the other arithmetic objects at the crate root implement Formula. Kernel runs these arithmetic objects at every float, complex and integer type, using the checking and wrapping policy specified by its Variant. For unbounded rationals, call Kernel::exact, which delegates to Formula::exact.
